questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to study law in French and I didn't want to go to France. I chose the university with the most EU law courses.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: We got a lot of information by e-mail over the summer (also in English), but as soon as we entered August, all information was available only in French, and the Erasmus-coordinator was only really approachable in French. We pieced our information together from the e-mails, what she told us, and (basically) rumors from other Erasmus students. It worked out in the end.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The e-mails, some office hours where we could go pick up our student card and some very basic info about the university. The Erasmus-coordinator was also available at other times, I went to see her in her office, but she didn't have hours, so you had to be lucky.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I knew of a company, Cohabs, that rents out rooms in big houses. I had a friend stay there when she was in Brussels, so I really only applied to that. The process was quite easy, but the options were quite expensive. I lived very close to campus (House was called La Cambre 138, situated by Roffiaen tram station), which was a big plus, but the living experience wasn't great, we had all sorts of issues – noise, not cleaning up after yourself, fly infestation and mice.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: For me it was a good solution, but it was expensive. I think I would have made more of an effort to find something private if I had to do it again, but that is also a risk. Some friends of mine who lived in dorms were happy with the price but said their conditions were also bad and people weren't that social.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was confusing at first and much more loose than at UCPH.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The term's (quadrimestre 1) courses were posted at the faculty's website. Through TimeEdit we could see when the classes took place. For the first 2-3 weeks we could go to any classes we wanted to, and by a deadline we had to let the Erasmus-coordinator know which courses we wanted to enroll in. It was very hard to make a schedule fit, and in the process we also discovered that not all professors accept Erasmus students. I ended up asking each professor ahead of the first class if I could join, and everyone accepted except one professor (Vaios Koutrolis for the courses in the Master de spécialisation droit international). I then wrote in the e-mail that I had gotten approval from all the professors, and I was enrolled in all the courses I wanted. For Public International Law, TP (travaux personnel, exercises) was mandatory, and enrollment into the groups/classes was done online, which was advertised as something very stressful we'd have to be very fast to get a spot in, but it wasn't a problem at all, in the end.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Not a lot, I went to the office of the Erasmus-coordinator a few times, but she couldn't do much, and then we went to some intro lectures for new bachelor students, but mostly we just figured it out on our own.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes I wanted. There were other courses I would have rather taken, but I couldn't make the schedule fit.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The first 3 weeks will be super stressful, but it will work out in the end. Get pre-approval for all the courses given at the faculty, so you don't have to worry about changing your pre-approval. I had to have mine changed but it was no problem.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level was lower than I had anticipated for most, but it was nice for settling in and understanding the style of teaching and adapting to the expectations – let alone get used to the language! The workload was bigger than at UCPH.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Much more sit-down-and-listen-style teaching at ULB. Most of it was lectures, where the professor half-heartedly said they wanted interaction, but the format wasn't right for it at all. In the seminar (TP) of Public International Law, we got grades for participation, so everyone was falling over each other trying to say something, which was a bad experience. In spite of the lively discussion, there was no room for being critical towards the curriculum, which I thought was a shame. In one class, Protection juridictionnelle dans l'Union européenne, the professor was very nice and actually encouraged participation. I participated the most in this class, in spite of my French not being perfect, and he was very supportive.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Protection juridictionnelle dans l'Union européenne (5 ECTS); Approches juridiques des discriminations (5 ECTS); EU Competition Law (5 ECTS); Droit de l'environnement (5 ECTS); Public International Law (10 ECTS)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Protection juridictionnelle dans l'Union européenne. It was a great course, I didn't learn a lot that I didn't know already from EU constitutional law or International dispute resolution and international courts (BA elective), but it was great for learning new perspectives and especially for learning the French vocabulary. The professor, Paul Dermine, was incredible, by far one of the best I've had all my years at university. He was patient and very encouraging of my French, and he spoke relatively slow and very clearly, so it wasn't too hard to follow. Bring your Uddrag af EU-retten book!

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I went to the doctor at the Services Medicales at the university, which I expected to be free, but the consultation (no add-ons) was 24 euros.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Groceries were expensive, but I guess they were also at home (inflation). I think you could definitely live for less money than I did, I just didn't want to think about expenses much. I rented a bike through Swapfiets which was the best spent money the whole time I was there. Eating out and take-away was less expensive.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I missed the friday bar at UCPH, at ULB they have préfab, which is friday bars in containers (yes) in the parking lot. It was fun in the summer but quickly got cold and the music wasn't very good. It was fun to experience the culture though, and the beer was much cheaper there than at UCPH.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Many! I was a part of ULB Sports, which cost 35 euros for the semester I think. I took some classes, it was very enjoyable.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: ULB Sports.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go to the nearby cities! You can get to Paris by direct train in about an hour and a half. I also went to Bruges. Some friends of mine also went to the mountains and to Amsterdam.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy because I had a good grasp of the language, but the culture itself was more difficult than I had expected. The level of politeness and the distance between professor and student made a much bigger impression on me than I had thought it would.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Take classes in French, especially from the Master de spécialisation droit européen. People were super nice, and the class was about half Belgian, quarter French, and the rest international, but most spoke English as well. I had luck with jumping into conversations with people complaining about the work, the programme, the professors or the university in general. Asking questions about the same things or admin/exam things that were foreign to me also worked. People were generally quite open and nice once you just initiated contact.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Knowing how polite to be and when to address someone by "vous" or "tu". In all my classes we had to address the professor by the formal you, but they in turn also addressed us the same, and as "madame", "monsieur" or "your colleague". In e-mails, I found out teachers want to be addressed by their title, e.g., Professor Dermine or Monsieur Professor Dermine. But they also know that you are not used to this, so you get the benefit of the doubt.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: All the Belgians I met were very open and helpful. The humor was quite similar to Danish, and I liked the culture of complaining. The food was also great.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: It will be stressful but it will work out and be worth it in the end. Have patience, the administration is *much* more messy than at UCPH. Try and spend less time stressing about academic work and grades, and go enjoy the time with your classmates.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: There's an intensive French course for 3 weeks in August, that helped me a lot.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I gained a lot more confidence from my stay. There were so many practical hurdles, but I overcame all of them. Also academically I feel more confident now. It was also an incredible full-circle moment to use the French I've spent the past 11 years learning, and I got more confident in speaking even though I'm still not fluent.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Adapting to the different teaching style and environment, all the practical issues, and homesickness.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
